1401.title: Gujarat's Swaminarayan
1401.hook: an old teacher calls himself only the drum-beater, and the young yogi from the road gets a new name
1401.howItsDone: Swaminarayan followers greet one another with 'Jay Swaminarayan' and chant the Swaminarayan mantra in daily worship, remembering how Ramanand Swami initiated Nilkanth as Sahajanand Swami.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujarat's Swaminarayan began with Nilkanth, the boy who walked across India with his questions until he reached the ashram at Loj.

Jay Swaminarayan. In Swaminarayan homes and temples, it's how followers of this tradition say hello, how they say goodbye, and often how they answer the phone. Two words, run together into one name. But whose name is it? The young yogi who walked into Loj didn't arrive with it. He was Ghanshyam as a child, Nilkanth on the road. Somewhere between that ashram and the greeting on the phone, a name was given, and then a mantra. Today, how the boy from the road became Swaminarayan.
screen: `JAY SWAMINARAYAN` → `A GREETING AND A NAME` → `WHOSE NAME IS IT?`

segments.voice: Ramanand Swami, whose ashram Nilkanth had reached, was a respected guru in Gujarat with followers of his own. When the two met, tradition says Ramanand saw something rare in the young man. He'd once described himself, the story goes, as only the drum-beater, the one who calls the crowd before the real performer arrives. Ramanand initiated Nilkanth as a sadhu and gave him a new name: Sahajanand Swami, the one whose joy comes naturally. Before long, he chose this newcomer to lead the whole fellowship after him. Tradition says that soon after Ramanand died, Sahajanand gave his followers a new name to chant: Swaminarayan. Swami, master. Narayan, a name of God. As people chanted it, they began to call him by it too. Here the communities that follow him say different things, and say them with care. For some, both words point to him: Sahajanand himself is Swami and Narayan, the Lord. For others, Swami names Gunatitanand Swami, whom they hold as the ideal devotee, and Narayan names Sahajanand, so the one name holds the ideal devotee and God together. They share the mantra, the greeting and the love for him. So this is a name that was given before it was worn, and chanted before it was explained. Now followers say it to each other at the door and on the phone.
screen: `RAMANAND, THE DRUM-BEATER` · `NILKANTH BECOMES SAHAJANAND` · `THE MANTRA: SWAMINARAYAN` · `ONE NAME, READ IN DIFFERENT WAYS`

segments.voice: Choose one name that matters to you, the name of God in your own tradition, a teacher, or a person you're grateful for, and say it inwardly on the in-breath, resting on the out-breath. When the mind wanders, come back to the name. If you pray in this tradition, you can use the mantra itself, Swaminarayan, as followers do.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, how Nilkanth became Sahajanand Swami under Ramanand, and how the mantra Swaminarayan became his name. Today's word.
Your line: Gujarat's Swaminarayan. A greeting that carries a name, and a name that carries a story. Until next time.

1402.title: Gujarat's Swaminarayan
1402.hook: a scripture made of questions asked out loud in a village courtyard
1402.howItsDone: In Swaminarayan mandirs and homes, passages from the Vachanamrut are read aloud and explained at gatherings, and devotees study it together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujarat's Swaminarayan: Nilkanth became Sahajanand Swami under Ramanand, and the mantra Swaminarayan became his name.

Evening in a village in Gujarat. A courtyard, a raised seat, a crowd on the ground: farmers, merchants, robed sadhus, children at the edges. The teacher on the seat is Swaminarayan, and he invites questions. Someone asks a hard one. Why does the mind keep running back to the same old cravings, even after years of devotion? He answers. Someone pushes back. He answers again. And off to one side, a few senior sadhus listen very closely, because they're going to write this down. Today, a holy book that began as a conversation.
screen: `A COURTYARD AT EVENING.` → `SOMEONE ASKS A HARD ONE.` → `SOMEONE WRITES IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: The book is the Vachanamrut. Followers hear the title as vachan, words, and amrut, the nectar of immortality: nectar in the form of words. They hold it as scripture, his own teaching, gathered from talks in Gadhada and other villages, each headed with the place, the setting, even what he was wearing that evening. First, its shape. It arrives as dialogue. A devotee asks, Swaminarayan answers, and sometimes he turns it around and asks the room, waiting to see who can answer. Learning happens in public, and sometimes the room has no answer to give. Then, the content. The questions are practical. How do you know if your devotion is real? What do you do with anger toward someone in your own community? Why does a person who has heard good teaching still not change? Kitchen-table questions, treated as worth a scripture. Last, the thread. Running through the answers is what tradition calls ekantik dharma, a whole-hearted life held up by four things together: dharma, doing what's right; knowing the self as distinct from the body; vairagya, detachment; and bhakti, love for God. Not one of them alone. All four lean on each other, like the legs of a cot. So a scripture of questions also trusts the people asking. The answers matter. So does the fact that someone was allowed to ask.
screen: `VACHANAMRUT — NECTAR IN WORDS` · `A SCRIPTURE THAT BEGINS AS DIALOGUE` · `KITCHEN-TABLE QUESTIONS` · `FOUR THINGS HELD TOGETHER`

segments.voice: Give one breath to each leg of the cot: doing what's right, knowing yourself as more than the body, letting go, and love, for one face or, if you pray, for God. Then notice, without judging, which leg feels steady today and which one wobbles, and rest on the whole cot for a few breaths.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, the Vachanamrut, his teaching kept as questions and answers from evening gatherings. Today's word.
Your line: Gujarat's Swaminarayan. In his courtyard, a hard question was welcome. See you tomorrow.

1403.title: Gujarat's Swaminarayan
1403.hook: a teacher writes a short letter of daily conduct for people he'll never meet
1403.howItsDone: The Shikshapatri asks Swaminarayan devotees to read it daily, and it is read aloud and explained at gatherings for those who listen rather than read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujarat's Swaminarayan and the Vachanamrut: a scripture that began as questions in a courtyard.

A conversation only reaches the people in the courtyard. So what about everyone else? The farmer three villages over who couldn't come. The family that moved away for work. The devotee born long after the teacher is gone. Swaminarayan's answer, tradition says, was a letter. Not a long book of philosophy: a short one, in verse, that a person could carry, read and live by. It's called the Shikshapatri. What makes it unusual isn't only what it says. It's how it asks to be used. Today, a letter written to people the writer would never meet.
screen: `THE ONES WHO COULDN'T COME.` → `A SHORT LETTER IN VERSE.` → `MEANT TO BE CARRIED.`

segments.voice: Shiksha means instruction, teaching. Patri is a letter. So the Shikshapatri is, plainly, a letter of instruction. Followers hold it as his own writing, and it reads like guidance from someone who knows what an ordinary day looks like. First, what it asks. In paraphrase, it asks followers not to harm living beings, not to eat meat or drink alcohol, not to steal, not to lie, and to be careful with harsh speech. It speaks of serving one's parents and giving to those in need. Much of it is everyday conduct: what you eat, how you speak, how you keep a household. Next, who it's for. Householders and sadhus, married women and widows, even rulers. It doesn't pretend everyone lives the same life; each gets guidance that fits. Last, how it asks to be used. The letter asks to be read every day, and for those who can't read, to be heard read aloud, with respect. So it carries its own instructions for staying alive. A teaching left on a shelf can fade. A teaching read every morning becomes part of the morning. That's the Shikshapatri's bet: small, steady contact with good words shapes a life more than one big moment of inspiration.
screen: `SHIKSHAPATRI — A LETTER OF INSTRUCTION` · `EVERYDAY CONDUCT, PLAINLY SAID` · `GUIDANCE THAT FITS EACH LIFE` · `READ IT EVERY DAY`

segments.voice: Bring back one line of good counsel you've been given, from a parent, a teacher, a book or a friend, in the words you remember. Say it once in your mind, then sit with it the way someone sits with the morning reading, bringing it back gently when it slips; if you pray, hold that line before God.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, the Shikshapatri, his short letter of everyday conduct, meant to be read, or heard, every day. Today's word.
Your line: Gujarat's Swaminarayan. A short letter, kept alive by being read each day. Until tomorrow.

1404.title: Gujarat's Swaminarayan
1404.hook: a whole community names itself after the company it keeps
1404.howItsDone: Swaminarayan devotees gather in weekly satsang assemblies at mandirs and in homes, with singing, readings from the scriptures and talks by sadhus or senior devotees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujarat's Swaminarayan and the Shikshapatri: a short letter of everyday conduct, meant to be read every day.

Ask a Swaminarayan devotee what they belong to, and you may hear a word this path met back on day twenty: satsang. Not a membership, not a congregation. A devotee is a satsangi. The weekly gathering is a satsang sabha. The whole fellowship, across Gujarat and in cities far from it, is spoken of as the satsang. It's an old Sanskrit word, used across Hindu traditions, and some families use it for a Sunday evening of singing in someone's living room. Here it names a whole community. Today, people named by the company they keep.
screen: `NOT A MEMBERSHIP.` → `SATSANGI, SATSANG SABHA.` → `NAMED BY THE COMPANY KEPT.`

segments.voice: The word comes apart in two. Sat is what is true, real and good. Sang is company, being together. So satsang is the company of the true, or of the good. It has three layers. First, the company of good people. In the Vachanamrut, Swaminarayan speaks about the company a seeker keeps, and how it shapes them. Ordinary life knows this. Spend your evenings with people who gossip, and gossip gets easier. Spend them with patient people, and patience rubs off. Satsang treats that as a spiritual fact, not just a social one. Second, the company of the holy. In this tradition, satsang especially means time near God and near a true sadhu, a holy person whose life shows the teaching. Being near such a person, listening, serving, watching how they handle an insult or a hard day, is itself a practice. Third, the company of good words. Satsang also happens when people gather to hear scripture read and explained, the Vachanamrut, the Shikshapatri, the songs of the tradition's poet-sadhus. Words become company too. So a community that calls itself the satsang is making a kind of promise: to keep good company, and to be good company for each other.
screen: `SAT — TRUE; SANG — COMPANY` · `GOOD PEOPLE RUB OFF` · `NEAR GOD AND A TRUE SADHU` · `GOOD WORDS AS COMPANY`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose company leaves you a little better, calmer, kinder, more honest, and notice what it is about them. Then bring to mind someone who might say the same about you, and let both sit with you for a few breaths, without judgment; if you pray, hold them both before God.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, satsang, the company of the true, the name the Swaminarayan community uses for itself. Today's word.
Your line: Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Here, a whole community is named for the company it keeps. See you tomorrow.

1405.title: Gujarat's Swaminarayan
1405.hook: a sadhu sings his teacher from head to foot, and the song is still sung after the evening lamps
1405.howItsDone: Swaminarayan devotees sing kirtans by the tradition's poet-sadhus at mandir gatherings and at home, including songs that describe Swaminarayan's form and his daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujarat's Swaminarayan and satsang: the company of the true, the name the community uses for itself.

A harmonium, a pair of small cymbals, a handful of voices in a mandir after the evening lamps. The song is a kind of portrait. It moves slowly over one person, the way an eye moves over a face it loves: the forehead, the eyes, the smile, the hands, the feet. The man who first sang it wasn't a painter. He was a sadhu, one of a circle of poets who traveled with Swaminarayan and turned what they saw into songs. Today, the last day in Gujarat: the poet-sadhus, and the songs they left behind.
screen: `AFTER THE EVENING LAMPS.` → `A PORTRAIT IN A SONG.` → `A CIRCLE OF POETS.`

segments.voice: Tradition remembers several by name. Muktanand Swami, the elder disciple who welcomed Nilkanth at Loj. Brahmanand Swami. Premanand Swami, a singer and musician. Nishkulanand Swami, who also told his teacher's life in the Bhaktachintamani. Their songs are still sung in Swaminarayan mandirs and homes. First, songs of watching. Tradition says Premanand sang Swaminarayan's form from head to foot, and the shape of his day: how he rose, how he bathed, how he sat with the people who came to see him. Devotees sing songs like these at night, so the day ends with the teacher close. A life remembered in loving detail becomes something to hold. Then, songs of longing, in the voice of a devotee who misses the beloved and can't bear the distance. Longing isn't a failure of faith here. It's part of love, and the poets give it a tune. Then, songs of letting go. Nishkulanand's verses press on vairagya, detachment. In paraphrase, one says that giving things up doesn't hold unless detachment has reached the heart. You can leave a house and still live in it in your mind. Set these beside the week: the Vachanamrut's questions, the Shikshapatri's letter, the satsang's company. The poet-sadhus gave something a child can learn by heart: a tune that carries the teacher's face and the teaching together. And that's where Gujarat ends: a boy on the road, a new name, a courtyard of questions, a letter, a company, and a circle of poets singing what they saw.
screen: `THE POET-SADHUS` · `SONGS OF WATCHING` · `SONGS OF LONGING` · `SONGS OF LETTING GO`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love, living or gone, or, if you pray, the form of God you pray to, and let your attention move over them the way the song does: the forehead, the eyes, the smile, the hands, one detail for each breath. When the mind wanders, come back to the last detail you saw. If missing someone feels heavy today, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, or call local emergency help.

1406.title: Punjab's shared devotional ground
1406.hook: a song from a Marathi tailor turns up in Punjab, and a boy keeps his eye on a kite string
1406.howItsDone: Namdev's hymns are sung by Varkaris in Maharashtra and, from the Guru Granth Sahib, in gurdwaras; in Ghuman, Punjab, a shrine honors him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujarat's Swaminarayan ended with the poet-sadhus, and their songs of watching, longing and letting go.

A boy on a rooftop is flying a paper kite. His friends are around him, laughing, teasing, talking over each other, and he's laughing with them. But watch his hands, his eyes. Whatever he's saying, part of him never leaves the string. That picture comes from a song by Namdev, the tailor-saint of Maharashtra this path met last year, singing to Vitthal. And the song is kept far to the north, in Punjab, in a book Sikhs honor as their living Guru. Today, Punjab, where devotional songs from many places ended up living side by side.
screen: `A BOY AND A KITE.` → `A SONG FROM MAHARASHTRA.` → `KEPT IN PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: Punjab is a crossroads, and the songs show it. First, the book. The Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs revere as their Guru, holds the hymns of the Sikh Gurus, and also songs by bhagats, devotees from outside that line: Namdev from Maharashtra, Kabir the weaver of Kashi, Ravidas, and Sheikh Farid, a Sufi of Punjab, among others. Sikhs sing them in the gurdwara beside the Gurus' own hymns. Hindus honor Namdev, Kabir and Ravidas in their own traditions too. So here is ground both share, each standing on it in its own way. Then, Namdev himself. Tradition says that late in life he traveled north and lived in Punjab, and a village there, Ghuman, remembers him with a shrine. A tailor from the Marathi country, honored in a Punjabi village. Songs travel with people, and sometimes people travel with songs. And now the kite. In paraphrase, the hymn gives a string of pictures. A boy flies his kite and talks with his friends, but his mind stays on the string. Young women carry water pots on their heads, laughing and chatting as they walk, but their attention stays on the pot. A cow grazes far out in the fields, her mind on her calf. A mother goes about her work, her heart on the child in the cradle. That, the song says, is how the mind can stay on God: not by stopping life, but in the middle of it. The talk goes on. Underneath, one thread holds.
screen: `PUNJAB, A CROSSROADS OF SONG` · `SAINTS FROM MANY PLACES IN ONE BOOK` · `NAMDEV REMEMBERED IN A PUNJAB VILLAGE` · `THE MIND ON THE STRING`

segments.voice: Let sounds come and go around you, traffic, voices, a fan, the way the friends chatter around the boy on the roof, and keep one light thread of attention on your breath, the way his fingers stay on the string. segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's shared devotional ground: Namdev's boy on the roof, laughing with friends, his mind on the kite string.

A small shop in Banaras. The smell of leather, a low bench, a man bent over a shoe with an awl in his hand. This is Ravidas, the cobbler-saint, whom this path first met on day ninety-five. A neighbor leans in the doorway. It's a holy day, he says. Everyone's going down to the Ganga to bathe. Come with us. Ravidas looks at the shoe in his hands. In one telling, he has promised it to a customer by tonight. Today, a cobbler who has to decide whether to put down his work.
screen: `A COBBLER'S BENCH IN BANARAS.` → `COME TO THE GANGA.` → `A SHOE PROMISED BY TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the story people tell. Ravidas doesn't go. He tells his neighbor, in a line people still quote: if the mind is pure, the Ganga is in this bowl, the leatherworker's bowl of water by his bench. In some tellings he gives the neighbor a coin to offer the river, but only if the Ganga reaches out and takes it herself. At the river, the story says, a hand rises from the water and takes it. First, the bench. The story isn't against pilgrimage. Ravidas honors the Ganga; that's why the coin goes. What it says is that the holy can't be kept from the bench of a man whose work others looked down on. Then, the song. His hymns are kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, and in one he sings of a city called Begampura, the town without sorrow. In paraphrase: no one there is anxious or afraid, no tax weighs on anyone, no one is ranked second or third, and anyone may walk where they please. A world where the cobbler and everyone else stand as equals. Last, Punjab. Ravidas lived in Banaras, but in Punjab you'll hear him called Guru Ravidas, and his birthday is kept with processions and hymn singing. Hindus honor him, Sikhs sing his hymns from their scripture, and communities who take his name honor him as their own Guru. Each comes to him in its own way. And the week behind: a courtyard of questions, a letter read each morning, the company of the true, the poet-sadhus' songs, a kite string, a cobbler's bowl. Every one sits close to an ordinary day.
screen: `IF THE MIND IS PURE, THE GANGA IS HERE` · `THE HOLY REACHES THE COBBLER'S BENCH` · `BEGAMPURA, THE TOWN WITHOUT SORROW` · `HONORED IN PUNJAB IN MANY WAYS`

segments.voice: Rest your hands where your work happens, on a desk, a counter or your knees, and think of the work in front of you this week, cooking, code, care, cleaning: let it be the bench. For a few breaths, treat this place as enough; if you pray, offer that work to God as it is, here, without going anywhere.
